..
Issued at 1200 PM CST Fri Nov 13 2026

After widespread dense fog Friday morning, midday visible
satellite imagery depicted an eroding stratus bank west of 
US 83. Sunshine will prevail this afternoon, although with
scattered cirrus increasing from the southwest, with
temperatures in the 50s. Midlevel height ridge axis will pass 
SW KS this evening, after which high and eventually midlevel
clouds will increase more quickly. NBM forecast minimum
temperatures Saturday may be a few degrees too cold, given 
elevated southeast winds and increasing mid/high clouds
interfering with radiational cooling. Most locations will 
be in the lower to mid 30s, just above freezing, 6 am Saturday. 

Models remain consistent with the track of the next negatively
tilted shortwave, from over the Great Basin 6 am Saturday, to
near northeast New Mexico 6 pm Saturday. Clouds will rapidly
increase Saturday in response to the improving forcing for
ascent, with rain breaking out south and west of Dodge City
Saturday afternoon. With thickening clouds and the onset of
rain, temperatures will be held in the 40s. The addition of 
an elevated raw moist southeast wind will make for a noticeably
November-like weekend. 

The majority of the rain will fall Saturday night, with rain
amounts of 1/4 to 1/2 inch common - greater with southern extent
toward Oklahoma, lesser with northern extent toward I-70. All
precipitation in Kansas will take the form of rain, with any wet
snow flakes restricted to the higher terrain of eastern
Colorado. 

The progressive shortwave will exit quickly Sunday early, taking
the rain with it. However, moist easterly upslope will be left
behind, and models agree stratus will hold all day Sunday. NBM 
was several degrees too warm Sunday given the anomalous cold 
set up, and along with neighboring WFOs, lowered Sunday's 
temperatures toward the colder MAV MOS guidance. GFS holds 
850 mb temperatures in the 1-2C range Sunday, and many 
locations will not get out of the 30s Sunday afternoon. Stratus 
are not expected to clear through Monday morning, which will 
work against any freeze concerns or frost formation, with 
temperatures essentially holding steady in the 30s. 

South winds return Monday, but this will be recirculated
continental polar air, and stratus will be very reluctant to
erode. This is often the case as we enter the shortest days of
the year with the weakest insolation. With some afternoon cloud
breaks, temperatures will struggle into the lower 50s Monday
afternoon. 

The next strong shortwave is forecast to reach California 6 pm 
Monday, eject through the Great Basin 6 pm Tuesday, and then
eject well to the north of SW KS Wednesday. This synoptic
evolution will create strong to intense south winds Tuesday and
Wednesday, and NBM wind grids were actually rather strong with
today's update. Gusts of 40-50 mph are likely each day.
Associated warm air advection will deliver a warming trend, with
widespread 60s Wednesday afternoon. Sustained south winds will
ensure the first widespread killing freeze of the fall season
will continue to be delayed. 

Friday through the pre-Thanksgiving weekend, the next stronger,
larger storm system remains apparent, but global models are out
of alignment, to be expected this far out. GFS is displaying its
progressive bias, while ECMWF's global ensemble members are
much, much wetter - with widespread significant rainfall
possible in Kansas November 20-22. NBM shows rapidly increasing
pops for rain next Friday, and this appears reasonable for now.  
Those making travel plans on the weekend before Thanksgiving 
should watch this storm system carefully. This system is still 
way out in the Pacific ocean; please follow trusted weather 
sources regarding this system as Thanksgiving approaches.
